# Mongolian language: an overview

Mongolian is the principal member of the Mongolic language family, spoken by
roughly five million people across Mongolia and the Inner Mongolia region. It is
notable for several interlocking features that make it a rich test case for a
knowledge base: two competing writing systems, a strict vowel-harmony system, a
highly agglutinative morphology, and an elaborate case system.

## Writing systems

Mongolian has historically used the traditional Mongolian script, a vertical
alphabet written top-to-bottom and left-to-right, derived from the Old Uyghur
script. In Mongolia, a Cyrillic alphabet was adopted in the 1940s and remains the
dominant everyday script, while Inner Mongolia continues to use the traditional
vertical script. The two systems encode the same language but differ sharply in
orthographic conventions, which matters for any translation or OCR pipeline.

## Vowel harmony

Mongolian vowels divide into front and back classes, and within a word the
vowels must agree in class — a phenomenon called vowel harmony. Suffixes
therefore have multiple surface forms and select the variant that harmonizes with
the stem's vowels. Rounding harmony adds a second dimension. Vowel harmony is the
single most pervasive phonological rule in the language and governs how nearly
every suffix attaches.

## Agglutinative morphology

Mongolian is strongly agglutinative: words are built by stringing together
clearly segmentable suffixes, each carrying one grammatical meaning. A single
verb stem can take a chain of suffixes marking voice, aspect, tense, and mood,
producing long but transparent word-forms. This regularity makes the morphology
learnable but interacts tightly with vowel harmony, since each appended suffix
must harmonize.

## Grammatical cases

Nouns inflect for a set of grammatical cases — nominative, genitive, accusative,
dative-locative, ablative, instrumental, and comitative — each marked by a
case suffix. Case marks the noun's role in the sentence and, like all suffixes,
the case ending harmonizes with the stem. The case system together with
postpositions carries most of the syntactic work that word order does in
English.
